_about: Concept ladder for the Learn stage. One concept per rung. Rung ids are progress keys: never rename. skills are glossary.json ids that move to Practiced when the check is passed. goals maps checkpoint data-ids to the rungs (1-based) that teach them. lang: c programs are compiled and run to verify each check.

rungs.title: Clone and pull
rungs.kick: git clone · git pull · git status · origin
rungs.builds: Phase 1: you already have the repo on your PC and have pushed to it. Now Person A needs their own copy.
rungs.why: You and Person A each keep a full copy of the game on your own PC. Clone makes that copy once. Pull brings in whatever the other person has pushed since. Skip the pull and you end up editing an old version of the game.
rungs.code:
rem Person A, once: copy Sam's repo to their PC
cd %USERPROFILE%\Documents\Dev
git clone https://github.com/4samtaylor/game-dev-exercises
cd game-dev-exercises
git log --oneline
rem Every session, before touching anything:
git pull
rem Already up to date.
git status
rem On branch main
rem Your branch is up to date with 'origin/main'.
rem nothing to commit, working tree clean
git remote -v
rem origin  https://github.com/4samtaylor/game-dev-exercises (fetch)
rem origin  https://github.com/4samtaylor/game-dev-exercises (push)
walk: git clone downloads the whole repo, with its full history, into a new folder named after it. You do this once per PC. Person A must be added as a collaborator on GitHub (Settings, then Collaborators) and accept the email invite before they can push. If the repo is private, they need this to clone it too.
The clone made a new folder. Step into it: git commands only work inside a repo folder.
git log --oneline lists the commits, newest first, one per line. Your Phase 1 commit is in there.
git pull asks GitHub for commits you don’t have yet and adds them to your copy. Make it the first command of every session.
When nothing new has been pushed, pull just says so.
git status tells you where you stand: which branch you're on (the Branches concept explains those), and whether you have changes.
“working tree clean” means every file matches the last commit. A good place to start work from.
git remote -v lists the remotes this repo knows. origin is the nickname clone gave the GitHub address, used for both fetching and pushing.
rungs.model: Mental model: a shared notebook. Clone is photocopying it once. Pull is copying in the new pages your partner wrote since you last looked.

check.q: Person A pushes a new commit at 3pm. At 4pm you run git log --oneline and nothing else. Does their commit appear?
opts: Yes, git log asks GitHub for the latest
Yes, because you cloned the repo earlier
No, not until you run git pull
No, not until you run git push
check.hint: git log reads your own copy. Which command updates your copy?
check.why: git log only looks at the copy on your PC. Their commit is on GitHub until you git pull it down. Push goes the other way: it sends your commits up.

miss.0: git log never contacts GitHub. It reads what’s already on your disk.
miss.1: Clone is a one-time copy. It doesn’t keep itself updated.
miss.3: Push sends your commits to GitHub. It doesn’t bring theirs down.

tryit.task: Fill in the commands: get the repo onto a new PC, then update it at the start of a later session.
tryit.answer: git clone (with the URL), and later git pull

qa: git status says “up to date” but Person A says they pushed.
status compares you with the last copy of GitHub your PC saw. It doesn’t check GitHub itself. Run git pull and it will catch up.
git pull says “Need to specify how to reconcile divergent branches”.
You and Person A both have commits the other lacks. Git needs a one-time setting to merge them. Merge conflicts shows it, and what happens next.
Clone asks me to sign in or says not found.
Person A isn’t a collaborator yet, hasn’t accepted the invite, or isn’t signed in to GitHub on that PC. Check Settings, then Collaborators, on the repo page.
What's in the hidden .git folder?

The whole history: every commit, every branch and the repo's settings. Your project files are one version laid out from it. Never edit inside .git, and never delete it, or the folder stops being a repo.
rungs.bridge: You can get the repo and keep it current. Next: .gitignore, so build files never get into the history you share.

parts: What a repo is

A repository (repo for short) is your project folder plus its whole history. The history lives in a hidden folder called .git at the top of the project: every commit, every branch and Git's settings for this project. The files you open and edit are the working tree, one version of the project laid out on disk so you can work on it.

That split explains a lot. Delete a .c file by accident and Git can bring it back from .git. Delete .git and the folder is just a folder again, with no history at all. You never edit anything inside .git by hand. File Explorer hides it; View, then Show, then Hidden items if you want to see it's there.
Three places your work can be

Every change you make passes through three places:

  1. Working tree: the files on disk. Saving in VS Code changes these and nothing else.
  2. Staging area: the changes you've picked for the next commit. git add runner.c puts a file's current state here.
  3. Repository: the commits inside .git. git commit turns everything staged into a new commit.

git status reports the gaps between them. “Changes not staged for commit” means edited but not added. “Changes to be committed” means staged. “nothing to commit, working tree clean” means all three agree.
What clone does

git clone does three jobs at once. It downloads every commit into a new .git folder, lays out the latest main as your working tree, and records where it came from under the name origin. origin is only a nickname for the GitHub address, so you don't have to type the URL again. git remote -v shows it.

Clone also makes origin/main: your PC's note of where GitHub's main was the last time the two talked. It's a bookmark, not a live view.
Why status can be out of date

git status and git log never contact GitHub. Status compares your main with origin/main, and that bookmark only moves when you fetch or pull. So “Your branch is up to date with 'origin/main'” really means “up to date with what I last heard”. If Person A pushed ten minutes ago, status won't know until you ask.

git pull is the asking. It contacts GitHub, downloads any new commits, moves origin/main, then brings those commits into your main. The Merge conflicts concept splits pull into its two halves.
Clone once, pull every session

Don't clone again to get your partner's changes. You'd end up with two folders, and sooner or later you'd edit the old one. Clone once per PC, then start every session with git pull inside that folder.
learn.king: Not in King; see Pro Git ch 1–3: 1.3 What is Git?, 2.1 Getting a Git Repository, 2.2 Recording Changes to the Repository, 2.5 Working with Remotes

rungs.title: .gitignore
rungs.builds: Phase 1: build.bat leaves .exe, .obj and .pdb files in your folder, and you met the three-line .gitignore. Clone and pull: from now on Person A gets whatever you commit.
rungs.why: Every build rewrites your .exe, .obj, .pdb and .ilk files. If any of them gets into Git, you and Person A will conflict over files neither of you can read, from the first day. A .gitignore tells Git to leave them alone, so set it up before you share any code.
rungs.code:
echo *.exe> .gitignore
echo *.obj>> .gitignore
echo *.pdb>> .gitignore
type .gitignore
rem *.exe
rem *.obj
rem *.pdb
git add .gitignore
git commit -m "chore: ignore build output"
rem runner.exe was committed before .gitignore existed:
git rm --cached runner.exe
git commit -m "chore: stop tracking runner.exe"
dir /b runner.exe
git check-ignore -v runner.obj
rem .gitignore:2:*.obj    runner.obj
walk: This writes one pattern per line into a file called .gitignore in the repo root. > creates the file, >> adds to it. In VS Code you can just create the file instead. Run this in the Developer Command Prompt, not Windows PowerShell 5.1: its echo writes UTF-16, which Git can’t read as patterns. (PowerShell 7 writes UTF-8 and is fine.)
type shows what you wrote.
*.exe means “any file ending in .exe”. Same for .obj and .pdb.
The .gitignore is itself committed, so Person A gets the same rules when they pull.
The catch: .gitignore only affects files Git isn’t tracking yet. A file already committed keeps being tracked.
git rm --cached removes it from Git’s tracking but leaves the real file on your disk.
The .exe is still in your folder. Git just stopped caring about it.

git check-ignore -v answers “which rule skips this file?”. It prints the file the rule is in, the line number, the pattern and the file name. No output means no rule matched, or Git already tracks the file.
rungs.model: Mental model: a “don’t photocopy these” list taped to the notebook. It works for pages not yet copied. Pages already in the book have to be taken out by hand.

check.q: runner.exe got committed before your .gitignore existed. You now add *.exe to .gitignore and rebuild. What does git status -s show for runner.exe?
check.hint: Think about which files .gitignore applies to.
check.why: Git already tracks runner.exe, so the ignore rule doesn’t apply to it. The rebuild changed it, so it shows as modified. git rm --cached stops the tracking.

miss.0: That’s what you’d get for an .exe that was never committed. This one was, so Git still watches it.
miss.2: ?? is for files Git has never seen. This one is in history.
miss.3: The rebuild replaced the file. Nothing deleted it.

tryit.task: Stop Git tracking game.pdb (already committed) without deleting the file.
tryit.code:
git ____ ____ game.pdb
git commit -m "chore: stop tracking game.pdb"

qa: What happens on Person A’s PC when they pull the “stop tracking” commit?
Git deletes runner.exe from their folder, since the commit removed it from the repo. They just rebuild with build.bat.
What else should be in it?
The starter list just below this concept also covers .ilk, .exp, .lib, .dll and build folders like Debug/. Paste it in your repo root.
I added a rule and nothing changed.
Check the file is named exactly .gitignore (no .txt on the end) and sits in the repo’s top folder. Then check whether the file was tracked before.
Why keep .exe, .obj and .pdb out of the repo?
They’re generated, so anyone can rebuild them in seconds. They’re binary, so Git can’t merge them, and every version is kept forever. Commit the recipe (your .c files and build.bat), not the cake.
What is a .pdb, and do I need it?

The program database: the debug information /Zi writes, which the debugger uses to match machine code to your lines and variable names. You need it on your disk to debug, but every build remakes it, so it stays out of Git.
rungs.bridge: Build output is out of the way. Next: writing good commit messages, so the history makes sense to both of you.

parts: Why this comes first

The first problem most pairs hit isn't a merge conflict, it's a committed .exe. One of you stages every changed file in one go, the build output goes in, and from then on every build changes files that both of you track. Those files are binary, so Git can't merge them, and every version stays in the history for good. Set up the .gitignore before you share any code and the problem never starts.
What a build leaves behind

With build.bat's /Zi flag, one build of runner.c leaves these next to your code:

  • runner.obj: the object file. cl turns each .c file into machine code here, then the linker joins the pieces.
  • runner.exe: the finished program the linker makes from the .obj files.
  • runner.pdb, plus one named like vc140.pdb (cl’s own default name): the program database. /Zi writes the debug information here, such as which line each instruction came from and your variable names. The debugger reads it.
  • runner.ilk: the incremental link file. /Zi turns on the linker's debug mode, and in that mode it keeps notes here so the next link can patch the .exe instead of starting over.

Every one of them is made from your .c files and build.bat. Delete them all and the next build puts them back.
How the patterns work

Each line of .gitignore is one pattern, checked against file names:

  • * matches any run of characters, so *.obj catches every object file in every folder.
  • A trailing slash means a folder: build/ skips the folder and everything in it.
  • ! brings a file back after a wider rule skipped it, like !.vscode/launch.json in the starter list.
  • A line starting with # is a comment.
Checking a rule works

git check-ignore -v runner.obj tells you which rule caught a file. It prints the .gitignore it came from, the line number, the pattern and the file name. If it prints nothing, no rule matched, or Git is already tracking the file, because tracked files are never ignored.
Already tracked means not ignored

A .gitignore only affects files Git isn't tracking yet. If runner.exe got committed before the rule existed, Git keeps watching it. git rm --cached runner.exe stops the tracking and leaves the file on your disk. Commit that, and the rule takes over from then on.
learn.king: Not in King; see Pro Git ch 1–3: 2.2 Recording Changes to the Repository (the part on ignoring files)

rungs.title: Writing good commit messages
rungs.kick: git diff · git diff --staged · HEAD · type: summary
rungs.builds: Phase 1: git add, git commit -m and git push. Clone and pull: the three places your work can be.
rungs.why: Once two people share a repo, the commit list becomes how you talk to each other. “fixed stuff” tells your partner nothing. A message that says what changed lets them know what to test, and lets you find a bug’s start weeks later.
rungs.code:
git status -s
rem  M runner.c
git diff
rem -    if (col > 0 && ducking) dodged = 1;
rem +    if (col >= 0 && ducking) dodged = 1;
git add runner.c
git diff --staged
git commit -m "fix: ducking now dodges obstacles at column 0"
git log --oneline
rem 3f2a1c9 (HEAD -> main) fix: ducking now dodges obstacles at column 0
rem 8b1e4d2 update
rem c07a9e5 stuff
walk: -s gives the short form of status: one line per changed file. The M in the second column means “modified, not yet staged”.
git diff shows the changes you haven't staged yet, line by line.
- is the old line, + the new one. Here > became >=, so column 0 now counts.
git diff --staged shows what's staged: exactly what the commit will hold. Plain git diff would now print nothing, because nothing is left unstaged.

The pattern is type: short description. feat is a new feature, fix a bug fix, refactor a restructure that changes nothing visible, docs readme changes, merge finishing a merge. Use double quotes in cmd.
HEAD -> main: HEAD is the commit you're on, reached through the main branch. The new commit reads well: you can tell what changed and what to test without opening the code.
What not to do. “update” could mean anything.
Same problem. In a month nobody can find which commit broke the jump.
rungs.model: Mental model: the caption on a photo. In a year, someone who wasn’t there should still know what the picture shows.

check.q: You fixed a bug where the player can jump twice in mid-air. Which message helps Person A most when they pull your commit?
opts: fixed the jump bug from yesterday
fix: player can no longer double-jump
feat: changed some stuff in player.c
check.hint: Pick the one that says what changed and what to test.
check.why: It has a type (fix) and says exactly what behaviour changed, so Person A knows what to try after pulling. It also reads clearly in git log months later.

miss.0: Better than nothing, but no type and no detail: fixed it how, and what should Person A test?
miss.2: One word. The log would be a column of these.
miss.3: It’s wrong as well as vague: this is a bug fix, not a feature.

tryit.task: You added a Player struct to the game code. Write the commit command with a good message.
tryit.answer: e.g. git commit -m "feat: add Player struct with x, y and lives"

qa: I made a typo in the message. Can I fix it?
Before you push, yes: git commit --amend -m "new message" replaces the last message. After a push, leave it. Rewriting shared history causes trouble.
Is there a rule about length?
Keep it to one line under about 70 characters. If you need more, a short message now and a note in the pull request (see Pull requests) works better.
Are there other types?
Teams add their own. chore (housekeeping like .gitignore) and test are common. Pick a short list with Person A and stick to it.
Why does Git make me git add before I commit?

So you choose what goes into each snapshot. If you fixed a bug and half-started a feature in one sitting, staging lets you commit just the fix with a message that says so. The staging area is the “this goes in the photo” pile.
What actually is a commit?

A full snapshot of every tracked file, plus a note of which commit came before it, who made it and why. The long hex string (a3f9c2e…) is a fingerprint of all that, so change one byte and it changes. That is why history can’t be changed without every later fingerprint changing too.
rungs.bridge: You can write messages worth reading. Next: branches, so new work doesn’t break the game both of you run.

parts: Look before you commit

A good message starts with knowing exactly what you're committing. Two commands show you:

  • git diff shows changes in your working tree that you haven't staged yet.
  • git diff --staged shows what you have staged: exactly what the next commit will hold.

Lines starting with - are the old version and lines starting with + are the new one. After git add runner.c, plain git diff goes quiet for that file, because nothing is left unstaged. That catches people out: the changes didn't vanish, they moved to the staging area. Press q if the diff opens in a pager and you want your prompt back.
HEAD

HEAD is Git's name for “the commit you're on right now”. Usually it points at a branch, and the branch points at its newest commit. That's why git log --oneline prints (HEAD -> main) beside the top line. When you commit, the new commit's parent is HEAD, and HEAD moves along to it. git diff --staged is really comparing the staging area with HEAD.
The message pattern

Write type: summary, one line, under about 70 characters. Your team's types:

  • feat a new feature, fix a bug fix
  • refactor a restructure that changes nothing visible
  • docs readme or comment changes, chore housekeeping like the .gitignore
  • merge finishing a merge, including the line you chose in a conflict

Write the summary as an instruction: “add jump”, not “added jump”. A handy test is that it should finish the sentence “If applied, this commit will…”.
Who made it

Every commit records a name and an email. Git takes them from two settings you make once per PC:

git config --global user.name "Sam Taylor"
git config --global user.email "you@example.com"

Use the email on your GitHub account, so GitHub can link each commit to your profile. git config user.email with no value prints the current setting.
Common slips

If Git opens a text editor when you run git commit, you forgot -m. Type the message on the first line, save and close. If the editor is Vim (a black screen with tildes), press Esc, type :wq and Enter.
learn.king: Not in King; see Pro Git ch 1–3: 1.6 First-Time Git Setup, 2.2 Recording Changes to the Repository, 2.3 Viewing the Commit History

rungs.title: Branches
rungs.kick: git switch -c · git switch · git branch
rungs.builds: Clone and pull: a repo with a clean main. Writing good commit messages: commits that say what they do, and HEAD.
rungs.why: If you both edit main directly, one half-finished feature can stop the game building for the other. The team rule is “main always builds”. Features get their own branch, and only come back when they work.
rungs.code:
git switch -c feature/jump
rem Edit and save jump.c, then:
git add jump.c
git commit -m "feat: add jump"
dir /b *.c
rem jump.c
rem runner.c
git switch main
dir /b *.c
rem runner.c
git branch
rem   feature/jump
rem * main
walk: git switch -c creates a new branch and moves you onto it. The name feature/jump says what the work is. Both branches start identical.
Staging the new file, exactly as in Phase 1.
This commit goes onto feature/jump only. main hasn’t moved.
dir /b *.c lists just the names of the .c files.
git switch main jumps back to main. Git rewrites your folder to match it.
jump.c is gone from the folder. It isn’t deleted: it’s safe in the feature/jump commit.
git branch lists branches. The * marks the one you’re on.
rungs.model: Mental model: a parallel draft of the story. Write freely in your copy. The published book (main) stays readable until your draft is ready.

check.q: Same session, but you save jump.c and forget git add and git commit. Then you run git switch main and dir /b. What do you see?
check.hint: A branch holds commits. Is jump.c in any commit yet?
check.why: A file Git has never added to a commit belongs to no branch, so it just stays in your folder when you switch. The danger: it looks like main has jump.c. Commit your work before switching so it stays with its branch.

miss.1: That’s what you’d see if jump.c had been committed on the branch. It wasn’t.
miss.2: Git only refuses when a switch would overwrite your uncommitted changes. A brand-new file doesn’t clash with anything.
miss.3: main’s files don’t disappear. runner.c is still there too.

tryit.task: Make a branch called feature/score, then go back to main.
tryit.code:
git ____ ____ feature/score
rem ...work and commit...
git ____ main
tryit.answer: git switch -c feature/score, then git switch main

qa: Can I commit straight to main?
Git lets you. The team rule is not to: main is always buildable and changes arrive through pull requests (next rung).
My Git says “switch is not a git command”.
Your Git is older than 2.23. Update Git for Windows, or use the old form git checkout -b feature/jump.
Does the branch exist on GitHub?
Not yet. It lives only on your PC until you push it. Pull requests does that.
Is a branch a copy of all my files?
No. It's a label pointing at one commit. Switching moves HEAD to another label and Git rewrites the files on disk to match that commit. Nothing is duplicated.
rungs.bridge: You can work on a branch. Next: pull requests, the way a finished branch gets back into main.

parts: A branch is a label

It's tempting to picture a branch as a copy of all your files. It isn't. A branch is a small label that points at one commit. main is a label. feature/jump is another. Making a branch writes one tiny file inside .git, which is why it's instant however big the game gets.
How the label moves

1. git switch -c feature/jump makes a new label on the commit you're on, and points HEAD at it.
  2. When you commit, the new commit's parent is the old one, and the label you're on slides forward to the new commit. Other labels stay put.
  3. git switch main points HEAD at main, and Git rewrites the working tree to match main's commit.

So after one commit on the branch, main and feature/jump point at different commits that share the same history up to the split. That's all a branch is: two lines of work that can grow apart and later join.
Uncommitted edits when you switch

Commits belong to branches. Edits you haven't committed belong to no branch, they're just in your working tree. When you switch:

  • If the files you changed are the same on both branches, Git carries your edits across. They now look like edits on main.
  • If a file you changed is different on the other branch, Git refuses: “Your local changes to the following files would be overwritten”. It won't throw your work away.
  • A brand-new file Git has never seen stays in the folder whichever branch you're on.

The safe habit: commit (or stash, with git stash) before you switch.
Throwing an edit away

git restore runner.c puts the file back to how it was at the last commit. Modern Git uses switch for branches and restore for files; older guides use git checkout for both.

restore can't be undone. Edits that were never committed or stashed are gone for good, so read git diff first.
Naming
Use feature/ for new work and fix/ for bug fixes, then a few words with hyphens: feature/duck-key. git switch - jumps back to the branch you were on before.

rungs.title: Pull requests
rungs.kick: git push -u · open PR · review · merge
rungs.builds: Branches: your feature/jump branch with a commit on it. Switch back to it if you're on main.
rungs.why: A branch is only on your PC until you share it. A pull request is the review step: Person A sees exactly what changed, plays it, comments, and merges it into main. That’s how main stays buildable with two people working.
rungs.code:
git switch feature/jump
rem ...edit, git add, git commit as usual...
git push -u origin feature/jump
rem GitHub prints a link. Open it and click Create pull request.
rem Person A reads the changes, plays the build, clicks Merge.
git switch main
git pull
git branch -d feature/jump
walk: git push -u origin feature/jump sends the branch to GitHub. origin is the name Git gives GitHub’s copy of the repo. -u links your branch to its twin there, so later a plain git push is enough.
The pull request is made on the GitHub website, not in the terminal. You describe what the branch does and pick Person A as reviewer.

The reviewer reads the diff on the Files changed tab (every changed line), can comment on lines, and when happy clicks Merge pull request. GitHub does the merge, in one of three ways depending on which merge button is picked. Learn it explains each one.
Back on your PC, move to main. Your local main is still the old one.
git pull brings down the merged result, so your main now has jump.c.
-d deletes your local copy of the branch. Git refuses if the branch has commits that exist nowhere else, so it’s a safe cleanup.
rungs.model: Mental model: handing Person A your draft and saying “read this before it goes in the book.” Nothing enters main until they’ve looked.

check.q: Person A clicks Merge on GitHub. Which step gets the new jump.c into the main on your PC?
opts: Nothing, GitHub updates your PC automatically
git switch main, then git pull
git pull while still on feature/jump
check.hint: GitHub merged into its main. Your main is a separate copy. How do you update it?
check.why: The merge happened on GitHub. To get it, be on main and pull. Your PC never updates itself.

miss.0: GitHub never reaches into your PC. You pull when you’re ready.
miss.1: That sends your branch up. It’s already there.
miss.3: That updates feature/jump, not main. The merged code lands on main.

tryit.task: After your PR is merged, update your PC and delete the branch.
tryit.code:
git ____ main
git ____
git branch ____ feature/jump
tryit.answer: git switch main, git pull, git branch -d feature/jump

qa: Do I have to wait for Person A every time?
For the shared game code, yes: that’s the point. For small notes or experiments you can agree to skip it. Settle that rule before you start.
git branch -d says “not fully merged”.

It means the branch has commits Git can’t find anywhere else, usually work you committed but never pushed. Push it first. If you’re sure you don’t need it (for example GitHub “squashed” the PR and deleted the branch), -D forces the delete.
Is there a way to open the PR from the terminal?
Yes, with GitHub’s gh tool: gh pr create --fill. You need to install gh first. The website is fine to start with.
How does Person A play my branch before merging?
On their PC: git fetch, then git switch feature/jump, then build. fetch downloads the branch, and switch makes a local copy that tracks it.
What do the three merge options mean?

Create a merge commit keeps every commit and adds a merge commit. Squash and merge rolls the branch into one new commit. Rebase and merge copies each commit onto main with no merge commit. The Learn it section has the detail.
rungs.bridge: You can get a branch reviewed and merged. Next: merge conflicts, which happen when you both change the same line.

parts: What a merge is

A merge takes the commits from one branch and joins them into another. It happens in one of two ways:

  • Fast-forward. If main hasn't moved since you made feature/jump, your branch is just main plus some commits. Git slides the main label forward to your newest commit. No new commit is made.
  • Merge commit. If main has moved on (Person A merged something), the two lines have grown apart. Git makes a new commit with two parents, one from each line, holding both sets of changes.

Either way, nothing is copied by hand and nothing on either branch is lost.
Reading a diff on GitHub

The pull request's Files changed tab shows every change. Red lines with - were removed, green lines with + were added, and plain lines around them are unchanged context. A header like @@ -40,6 +40,9 @@ means “starting at line 40, 6 lines became 9”. Click the + beside a line to leave a comment on it. Review for one thing at a time: does it build, does it do what the title says, is anything in there that shouldn't be?
Playing your partner's branch

Reading isn't testing. To run Person A's branch on your PC:

git fetch
git switch feature/duck
build

git fetch downloads their branch without touching yours. git switch with the branch name then makes a local copy that tracks theirs. Play it, then git switch main when you're done.
GitHub's three merge buttons

The arrow beside the green button offers three choices:

  • Create a merge commit: always adds a merge commit, even when a fast-forward would do. The history shows exactly when each branch came in.
  • Squash and merge: rolls all the branch's commits into one new commit on main. Tidy, but the separate steps are gone from main.
  • Rebase and merge: copies each commit onto the end of main one by one, with no merge commit. The copies get new hashes.

Pick one with Person A and stick to it. Create a merge commit is the easiest to follow when you're starting out.
After the merge
After a squash or rebase merge, git branch -d may say the branch is “not fully merged”, because main holds copies, not your original commits. Check the PR shows Merged, then use -D.

rungs.title: Merge conflicts
rungs.builds: Clone and pull, Branches and Pull requests: pulling, two copies that drift apart, and what a merge is.
rungs.why: Git merges most changes by itself. When you both change the same line, it can’t guess whose is right and stops. It’s normal, not a disaster. Practise on purpose now, so the first real one doesn’t feel like an emergency.
rungs.code:
git config --global pull.rebase false
git pull
rem CONFLICT (content): Merge conflict in runner.c
rem Automatic merge failed; fix conflicts and then commit the result.
type runner.c
rem <<<<<<< HEAD
rem #define FRAME_MS 20
rem =======
rem #define FRAME_MS 16
rem >>>>>>> cb284f65b60eec7847a6ee9ebcc097c1b9354948
rem Edit runner.c: keep one line, delete all three marker lines
git add runner.c
git commit -m "merge: keep 16ms frame time"
git push
walk: One-time setting so git pull merges. Without it, newer Git refuses when both sides have new commits. Git for Windows usually sets this at install; running it again is harmless.
Git tells you which file clashed and that the merge is paused. Nothing is lost. Run git status any time: it lists the file as both modified.
type shows the file. Git has written both versions into it.
<<<<<<< HEAD starts your version: what you had committed locally.
======= is the divider between the two versions.
>>>>>>> ends their version, the one from GitHub. After it you’ll see a commit id or branch name.
The fix is by hand: pick one line (or write a blend) and delete the marker lines. In VS Code, Accept Current Change keeps yours and Accept Incoming Change keeps theirs.
git add tells Git “this file is resolved”. git commit finishes the merge, then push shares it.
rungs.model: Mental model: two editors rewrote the same sentence. Git can’t pick the wording, so it pastes both and asks you to choose.

check.q: In the conflicted runner.c above, which line is the one you committed on your own PC?
check.hint: Which marker starts the block with your commit?
check.why: The line between <<<<<<< HEAD and ======= is your side. Below ======= is the incoming change from Person A. If you left the markers in, the file wouldn’t compile.

miss.0: That’s below the =======: the incoming side, Person A’s commit.
miss.1: Only one is yours. The other is theirs, which is why they clash.
miss.2: That line is a marker, not code. It just starts your block.

tryit.task: You chose to keep Person A’s value. Finish the steps after editing runner.c.
tryit.code:
rem runner.c now has only #define FRAME_MS 16
git ____ runner.c
git ____ -m "merge: keep 16ms frame time"
git ____
tryit.answer: git add runner.c, git commit -m "...", git push

qa: I’m scared I’ll lose work. How do I back out?
Run git merge --abort. It puts everything back as it was before the pull. You can try again calmly.
What if I leave the markers in and build?
The compiler stops with errors, because <<<<<<< isn’t C. Search the file for it before you commit.
How do I avoid conflicts?
Pull often, keep commits small, and tell each other which file you’re in. You can’t avoid them forever, and that’s fine.
Why is there a merge commit I didn't write?
pull is fetch plus merge. If you both committed since your last pull, the merge can't just slide main forward, so Git makes a merge commit for you. That's normal.

parts: pull is two steps

git pull is really two commands run back to back:

  1. git fetch downloads new commits from GitHub and moves origin/main. Your files don't change.
  2. git merge origin/main joins those commits into your current branch, exactly like the merges in Pull requests.

If you both committed since you last pulled, the merge can't fast-forward, so Git makes a merge commit. That's the “Merge branch 'main' of github.com/…” commit you didn't write. It's normal.
How Git spots a conflict

Git finds the last commit both sides share, then looks at what each side changed since. Changes in different places combine on their own. If both sides changed the same lines, or lines right next to each other, Git can't know which you want, so it stops and asks. Most merges never conflict at all.
Where you stand mid-conflict

git status is your map while a merge is paused. It says “You have unmerged paths”, lists each clashing file as both modified, and reminds you of the two ways out: fix the files and commit, or git merge --abort to go back to how things were before the pull. Files that merged cleanly are already listed as staged.
Fixing it in VS Code

Open the file and VS Code colours the two sides. Above the markers it shows small buttons:

  • Accept Current Change keeps your side (the HEAD block).
  • Accept Incoming Change keeps their side.
  • Accept Both Changes keeps both, one after the other. You'll usually need to tidy the result.
  • Compare Changes shows the two side by side.

Then build and run before you commit. A file with no markers can still be wrong. Finish with git add on the file and git commit, using a merge: message.
Rebase, in two lines

You'll see git pull --rebase online. It replays your commits on top of theirs instead of making a merge commit, which keeps history in a straight line but rewrites your commits. This course sets pull.rebase false so pull always merges.
The editor that pops up
When pull makes a merge commit on its own, Git may open a text editor for the message. The default message is fine: save and close. If it's Vim, press Esc, type :wq and Enter.
